text:
And he thought of putting out the light in the room so as to have more courage,
but he wanted a glimmer to filter in, a half-light gradually becoming more
discernible, perhaps from the streetlamps on the road, perhaps from a shaded lamp
in the adjoining room. And he smelled the diffused scent of her body,
that same scent, but sweeter, which she had on her mouth when kissing him; an
intense and manifold scent that blossomed from her skin, as though roses were
hidden in the folds of her body. He savored the freshness
of that springtime flesh, imagined caressing her round
bare shoulder, slipped his groping hand into the velvety warmth of her
armpits, gathered her torso, supple as a young shoot, into his clasping arms,
felt against himself the unrestrainable throbbing of
her womb, the entwining her body would make against his
body, in order to offer herself and defend herself, conceived the savage joy of
being able to stun her, heard in her throat the death rattle of her fleeing virginity,
heard her weep in ecstasy, laugh in pain... then he
saw her as she was, slender, arched, strong in her slightness, turning pale for a
moment with that pallor which is close to death, and flashing forth in all her beauty
with love in that exultant hatred with which the virgin gives herself...

But suddenly she had felt ill. Truly, as in his
vision, he had seen her blanch with that same pallor, had felt
her convulsive hands seize his arms, then, seeing her
stagger, had supported her against himself.

“What is wrong, Lora?”

She did not answer; her teeth were chattering; she was trembling.

“Lora! Lora! What is wrong?”

“Nothing...” she stammered, “it will pass...”

It was only dizziness, and her mouth soon smiled at him again. They retraced
their way; he supported her as far as the carriage.

The coachman chattered; the little horse began trotting again toward the city
of its martyrdom, where there were rough stone, slippery rails,
the stand, and the stable. On either side of the two hedges, fragrant in the
white night, the tilled earth was growing grain and fruit for the
voracious city; some cricket enamored of the moon raised its shrill song,
infinitely greater than itself.

Now her head hurt; around her temples she had an iron band that
hammered. To soothe that pain she took one of her brother’s hands and
bound her forehead with it.

“Are you suffering?”

“Yes, a little.”

He encircled her forehead, from one temple to the other, with so many little
kisses.

“Hold me close, very close... and I shall recover.”

In a garden they passed, the roses of May were opening their
calyxes swollen with spring.

“Do you still feel ill?”

“Yes, a sweet pain...”

Beyond a row of poplars there reappeared, like a vast cloud suspended
in the firmament, the red blaze of the city. They came upon the first
houses, with walls white in the moonlight. Now the crickets were a hundred, were
a thousand, lost in the May hay, and one, more wrathful than all the rest,
seemed to pursue them close at hand along the hawthorn hedge.

All at once she let her head fall back against his shoulder, as though the onset
of a faint were overpowering her.

“Rigo, I feel ill...” she stammered, pressing her breast.

“But what is wrong?” he said, bewildered. “Why are you suffering so?”

She closed her eyes and still tried to smile at him from her wholly white face.

“I feel dizzy... I do not know...”

“Do you want to stop? What do you want to do?”

“Nothing; it will pass now... it will pass... I love you...”

When they reached the last farmhouse, the cricket’s wandering song
faded far away, infinitely far away, and died. But ahead there appeared
the monumental customs gate, majestic as a triumphal arch beneath the starry sky.
The customs guards, seated beside the booth, laughed and smoked, chatting
with women of ill repute. Amid throngs of children, some vagrants
were playing in a street vendor’s raffle; a swallower of burning tow gaped
his enormous soot-blackened mouth before the astonished spectators.

“I love you...” she said again, in a breath, to her pale lover.

And the hair shirt of the inexpiable sin clothed their desperate flesh like a
mantle of thorns.




VIII


He arrived unexpectedly at Clara Michelis’s house around lunchtime.
For several days she had not seen him; she had written to him
several times without receiving an answer, had repeatedly gone to his house, but
without ever finding him. She could not regard it as unusual that
Arrigo should neglect her; yet he had never shown himself indifferent to such a degree.

Mother and daughter were sitting at the table when he arrived. It was the
servant who first asked him whether he had already had lunch.

After he answered no, his usual place was laid for him, and there he
sat down with the air of a broken man.

“I have had a great deal to do these past few days,” he said by way of apology. “Forgive me for not coming.”

Neither the daughter nor the servants were any longer surprised at his presence
in that house; he had become somewhat its master, everyone knew in what capacity,
and by now no one paid any attention to it. That day his
face was pale and agitated, his eyes full of fever, his hands somewhat restless.

“I have been extremely busy,” he repeated, as though he did not know what else
to say.

Out of regard for her daughter, Clara did not answer a word, but remained
watching him, staring at him, with her gentle eyes full of tenderness and
resignation. She was greatly afraid of him when she saw him arrive in
that state. She too looked worn, and since she had expected to be alone,
she had come to lunch in a dressing gown without having finished doing herself up.
The face powder left a visible trace on her somewhat worn skin;
her neck, which emerged slenderly from the lace of her neckline,
had the appearance of something sickly; as she ate, a few very faint
wrinkles formed at the corners of her mouth and near the arches of her
eyebrows. Perhaps she had wept during the sleepless night; her eyes
seemed to have grown dim, and they turned toward her lover a gaze full
of anguished sweetness.

Adelina, on the other hand, appeared entirely fresh in her blooming seventeen years;
but that Signor Arrigo made her somewhat uncomfortable when, instead of joking
with her as usual, he came with that mastiff-like face of his
and from time to time looked at her with his violent eyes, like those of a
nocturnal bird of prey.

“What could you possibly have had to do all these days?” Clara finally
asked, trying to give her words a playful tone.
